source-support-radial-positive-site: A site is the smallest visible participant: a place that can be read before a direction or length is chosen. In this row the site is treated as a source whose flow moves outward.
source-support-radial-positive-flow: Positive radial flow leaves the site in every available direction. It is unbounded here, so the diagram shows influence rather than a finished shape.
source-support-radial-positive-boundary: A second mark can turn outward flow into a measured boundary. The dashed radius is the evidence connecting the site to that boundary.
source-support-radial-positive-bounded-s: Once a radial boundary is filled, the inside becomes support. Positive support means the bounded surface participates with the outward sense.
source-support-radial-positive-partition: Partition marks make the boundary readable in repeated steps. The circle is no longer only a limit; it can be counted, compared, and revisited.
source-support-radial-positive-orientati: Orientation chooses which way counts as positive around the boundary. Here the positive radial row uses counterclockwise order, so later direction reads can place positive and negative sides consistently.
source-support-radial-positive-direction: Direction starts from a zero position on the boundary. With this orientation, positive moves away from zero counterclockwise while negative flows back into zero from the opposite side.
source-support-radial-inverse-site: The same site can be read with the opposite sense. Nothing about the point changes; only the chosen flow sense changes.
source-support-radial-inverse-flow: Inverse radial flow moves toward the site from its surroundings. The site becomes the place where incoming change gathers.
source-support-radial-inverse-boundary: The inverse boundary uses the same measured distance but reads the opposite face. The circle is still the limit; the red sense marks which side is emphasized.
source-support-radial-inverse-bounded-su: The inverse fill keeps the same boundary but gives the support the opposite sense. The structure is stable enough to be occupied, compared, or carried forward.
source-support-radial-inverse-partitione: Inverse partitioning keeps the same repeated boundary marks under the opposite sense. The ticks belong to the boundary, while the color shows how the boundary is being read.
source-support-radial-inverse-orientatio: The same boundary can choose clockwise order as its positive orientation. This reverses where positive and negative direction appear without changing the underlying circle.
source-support-radial-inverse-direction: Direction is still measured from zero, but the chosen orientation is reversed. Positive now moves away from zero clockwise, while negative flows into zero from the other side.
source-support-linear-site: Two nearby sites can be read together before a line is fully named. Their relation gives the next diagram enough structure to stretch between them.
source-support-linear-flow: A linear pair can emit flow on the side perpendicular to the line between its sites. The two colored directions show the two opposite sides of that same line.
source-support-linear-boundary: Two sites can bound a segment. The dashed evidence says this is a measured span rather than a free-floating pair.
source-support-linear-bounded-support: A segment can support different sides. The center line remains the boundary while the colored bands show the two available faces.
source-support-linear-partitioned: Ticks partition a segment from inside its own span. The marks are not new points by themselves; they are readable positions along the bounded structure.
source-support-linear-orientation: A line can choose rightward or leftward as its positive orientation. The selected orientation tells later reads which side of zero should count as positive.
source-support-linear-direction: Direction on a line is read from a zero point. Positive moves away from zero in the chosen orientation, while negative flows into zero from the opposite side.
direction-area-radial-positive-direction: A direction can be chosen from a radial site even though the site itself has no preferred direction. The choice gives one local path and leaves the opposite sense available.
direction-area-radial-positive-boundary-: Boundary support fills the radial limit with the positive sense. The edge still carries the measured boundary, while the interior becomes available support.
direction-area-radial-positive-directed-: A directed boundary is a portion of the circular limit with an order. The endpoint and arrow show where the read enters and how it proceeds.
Directed support fills the swept portion of the boundary. The region participates with the same order as the directed edge.
direction-area-radial-positive-area: An area is support that can be read as occupied rather than only edged. At this stage the shape is present even if no directed area has been selected.
direction-area-radial-positive-area-face: A filled area can also carry spin around its own boundary. Positive spin gives the face an ordered way to circulate.
direction-area-radial-positive-directed-: A directed area gives the occupied face a circulating read. The area remains bounded, but the face now has a positive order around its edge.
direction-area-radial-positive-bounded-a: A bounded area keeps the fill, partitioned boundary, origin, and full radius readable together. The shape is no longer just occupied; its limit and directed face behavior are both present.
direction-area-radial-inverse-direction: The inverse radial direction chooses the opposing sense from the same site. The source stays fixed while the read turns inward or around the other way.
direction-area-radial-inverse-boundary-s: Inverse boundary support fills the same radial limit with the opposite sense. The support is stable, but its face is read from the inverse side.
direction-area-radial-inverse-directed-b: An inverse directed boundary uses the same circular limit with reversed order. The red edge marks that the boundary is being followed in the opposite sense.
direction-area-radial-inverse-directed-s: Inverse directed support fills the swept region under the reversed read. The region is structurally similar to the positive case but carries the opposite sense.
direction-area-radial-inverse-area: The inverse area is occupied support with the opposite face selected. The filled shape is stable; the color tells how it participates.
direction-area-radial-inverse-area-face-: Inverse spin gives the filled face the opposite circulation. This makes the face readable as more than a filled outline.
direction-area-radial-inverse-directed-a: An inverse directed area gives the occupied face clockwise circulation in this row. The boundary is the same kind of structure, but the face turns in the opposite sense.
direction-area-radial-inverse-bounded-ar: An inverse bounded area keeps its fill, partitioned boundary, origin, and full radius together under the inverse read. This makes the opposite face inspectable rather than just differently colored.
direction-area-linear-direction: On a line, direction runs along the bounded span. Choosing a direction makes one end behave as the start of the read.
direction-area-linear-boundary-support: Boundary support on a line separates the two faces held by the segment. The line remains the divider while the supported sides become readable.
direction-area-linear-directed-boundary: A directed segment is the bounded span with an ordered read. The start point is now meaningful because the segment has a chosen direction.
direction-area-linear-directed-support: Directed linear support keeps the line as the divider while each face has its own directional read. The two faces can carry opposite motion without changing the segment.
direction-area-linear-area: A linear boundary can produce side areas. The separated bands show the positive and inverse faces as distinct occupied supports.
direction-area-linear-area-face-spin: Side areas can carry directed motion along the line that bounds them. The upper and lower faces keep opposite senses while sharing the same structural divider.
direction-area-linear-directed-area: A directed area on linear support appears as motion along the faces of the segment. The two sides can circulate in opposite senses while sharing the same divider.
direction-area-linear-bounded-area: A bounded linear area closes the side support into an inspectable region. Its fill, surrounding edge, and face direction can all be read together.
curves-line-line-corner: A corner joins two line carriers without smoothing the change in tangency. The join is structural and visible as a cusp rather than a plotted bend.
curves-line-line-arc-blend: An arc blend rounds the turn between two line carriers. The curve belongs to the joining relation, while the gray lines remain the carriers being joined.
curves-line-line-bezier: A Bezier join uses tangent evidence from both line carriers to shape a smooth bridge. The handles show that the curve is guided by carrier direction rather than by a table of plotted points.
curves-line-line-clothoid: A clothoid-like join changes curvature gradually as it leaves one line and settles toward the next. The small normal ticks suggest curvature increasing through the join.
curves-line-line-involute: An involute-like join unwinds from a local support while crossing between line carriers. The curve is still a carrier join, not a Cartesian function drawn over axes.
curves-line-line-plotted: A plotted path is shown as a contrast case. Here the curve is sampled through positions on axes, which can look similar but is conceptually different from joining carriers by tangency.
curves-line-arc-corner: A line can meet an arc with a sharp cusp when the tangent direction changes suddenly. The join is valid structure, but the discontinuity remains visible.
curves-line-arc-arc-blend: An arc blend can bridge a line carrier into an arc carrier. It smooths the transition by using the outgoing line direction and the incoming arc tangency.
curves-line-arc-bezier: A Bezier bridge can join a line to an arc by reading the tangent at each end. The control handles are local evidence for how the join leaves one carrier and enters the other.
curves-line-arc-clothoid: A clothoid-style bridge is useful when a line needs to become curved gradually. The curvature grows through the join instead of appearing all at once.
curves-line-arc-involute: An involute-like bridge can unwind into an arc carrier. The base support hints that the curve is generated from a relation between carriers, not just plotted coordinates.
curves-line-arc-plotted: The plotted version samples positions between the same visual endpoints. It can mimic a line-to-arc join, but the drawing is organized around points on axes rather than carrier tangency.
curves-arc-arc-corner: Two arc carriers can meet sharply when their tangencies do not settle into one another. The cusp records that the join is sudden rather than smooth.
curves-arc-arc-arc-blend: An arc blend can smooth the gap between two arc carriers. The bridge reads the direction of each arc at the join and supplies a rounded transition.
curves-arc-arc-bezier: A Bezier bridge can join one arc carrier to another through their endpoint tangencies. The handles make the tangency evidence visible without requiring a Cartesian plot.
curves-arc-arc-clothoid: A clothoid-like bridge changes curvature between the two arc carriers. This is useful when the join should feel gradual rather than a fixed-radius patch.
curves-arc-arc-involute: An involute-like bridge can unwind between curved carriers. The local support circle shows a generating relation that is separate from either carrier alone.
curves-arc-arc-plotted: The plotted contrast samples positions through a curve between the arc endpoints. It may resemble a carrier join, but its meaning comes from sampled positions rather than joined tangency.
branches-tip-branch: A branch can split from the tip of an existing carrier. The join point records that the new carrier participates with the old one rather than merely passing nearby.
branches-tip-merge: A merge gathers two incoming tips into one outgoing carrier. The common point is the structure that makes the gathered flow inspectable.
branches-tip-orthogonal-joint: A butt joint and a corner both show sudden settlement at a tip. The incoming carrier can arrive from an orthogonal direction and create a hard change rather than a smooth curve.
branches-tip-other: An arc can branch from a carrier tip just like a segment can. The curved carrier is joined by tangency or force, not by plotting coordinates.
branches-middle-branch: A branch can also begin in the middle of a carrier. The orthogonal force marks that the new carrier emerges from the side rather than from an endpoint.
branches-middle-merge: A middle merge lets orthogonal carriers gather into an existing carrier. The trunk continues while the join point remains locally readable.
branches-middle-orthogonal-joint: An arc can enter the middle of a carrier from an orthogonal direction. This kind of join can be smooth or abrupt depending on how the joining relation settles.
branches-middle-other: A crossing is not automatically a join. Two carriers can occupy the same visual region while remaining separate structures.
branches-structure-branch: More than two branches can share one point. The hub is a local branching structure, not a special global node type.
branches-structure-merge: A larger branch structure can split and later merge again. The route is made of local joins whose evidence remains visible at each settlement point.
branches-structure-orthogonal-joint: A closed set of joined carriers can create area, including an area with a curved side. The separate branch line shows that a nearby carrier does not participate in the fill unless it joins the enclosure.
branches-structure-other: A U shape can imply a partial inside and outside even when one boundary is poorly defined. The dashed side marks that the area is readable but not fully settled, while the separate branch line remains unrelated.
point-site: A point or site is the smallest rendered carrier position. It is visible because the structure provides a place that can be read.
point-pair: Two points give a read something to compare. Before a segment is named, the pair already suggests separation and possible span.
segment: A segment is the bounded stretch between two readable sites. It carries length because the endpoints hold the span in place.
directed-segment: A directed segment keeps the same bounded stretch and adds an ordered read. One end acts as the start, and the other acts as the direction of travel.
radial-flow: Radial flow shows influence leaving or entering a site. It does not yet end at a boundary, so it remains open structure.
line-seed: A line seed begins from structure that can extend beyond the visible mark. It is useful when the relation matters more than the clipped drawing.
sheet-seed: A sheet seed suggests support emerging from a bounded linear mark. The rendered shape hints at the next dimension without requiring a full area object.
circle: A circumference is a radial boundary held at a consistent distance from a site. It marks a limit without filling the interior.
radius: A radius attachment shows the evidence that ties a center to a boundary point. That evidence is what makes the circular limit readable.
arc: An arc is a portion of a circular boundary. It has a start and end on the same boundary rather than a complete circumference.
quadratic: A quadratic curve bends through one control site between its endpoints. The control site shapes the path without becoming an endpoint.
cubic: A cubic curve uses two control sites to shape a path between endpoints. This gives the bend separate entry and exit behavior.
segment-partitions: Segment partitions mark readable positions inside a bounded span. They let the same segment be counted or compared at a chosen resolution.
contour-partitions: Contour partitions mark repeated positions along a circular or curved boundary. The boundary stays continuous while the read gains steps.
area-fill: An area fill treats a closed boundary as occupied support. The fill is the participation of the inside, not just a visual color.
anti-area-fill: An anti fill reads the opposite face of the same closed support. It keeps the boundary but changes which side participates.
closed-boundary: A closed boundary returns to itself and can hold an inside and outside apart. This makes it ready to support area reads.
area-union: An area union combines participating regions into a single readable surface. The outline shows the settled result of that combination.
outline-witness: An outline witness records the boundary evidence for an area read. It lets the rendered edge remain inspectable after the fill is understood.
path-branch: A branch path lets one incoming span continue into more than one outgoing span. The shared site is the place where the structure splits.
path-merge: A merge path lets multiple incoming spans settle into one outgoing span. The shared site is the place where the structure gathers.
shared-polyline: A shared polyline is several connected spans read as one route. Each joint remains local evidence inside the larger path.
selection: Selection evidence marks a source and a matched read without hiding the relation between them. It is useful when the chosen structure needs to stay inspectable.
